<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
Let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ satisfy \eqref{eq:displacement} with $1\le q<2$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset E_q$, and $T$ is a Ritt operator if and only if $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$;
\item $T$ is a $\mathrm{Ritt}_{E_q}$ operator with $K_{E_q}(T)\le\Phi(q)$, where $\Phi(q)$ depends only on $q$; consequently $T^{N(q)}$ is a Ritt operator with $C_{\mathrm R}(T^{N(q)})\le N(q)\Phi(q)$;
\item for $L\ge1$, the implication ``\eqref{eq:displacement} $\Rightarrow$ $T^L$ is Ritt'' holds on every Banach space if and only if $N(q)$ divides $L$;
\item if $q<\sqrt3$, then $E_q=\{1\}$, $T$ is a Ritt operator, and
\[
C_{\mathrm R}(T)\le\frac{2\sqrt3 M(T)}{\sqrt3-q}
          \le\frac{6+2\sqrt3}{\sqrt3-q}.
                                 
\]
                                                                                                 
Define the optimal universal bound by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:optimalPhi}
 \Phi_*(q):=\sup\left\{C_{\mathrm R}(S):
 \begin{array}{l}
 Y\text{ a complex Banach space},\quad S\in\mathcal B(Y),\\
 \displaystyle\sup_{n\ge1}\|I-S^n\|\le q
 \end{array}\right\},
 \qquad 1\le q<\sqrt3.
\end{equation}
Then $\Phi_*(q)<\infty$, the threshold $\sqrt3$ is sharp, and
\[
 \Phi_*(q)=\frac{2}{\sqrt3-q}+O(1)
 \qquad(q\uparrow\sqrt3).
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- theoremb-1: body_md -->
Let $X$ be uniformly convex and let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ be a contraction. The following assertions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\sup_{n\ge1}\|I-T^n\|<2$;
\item $T^N$ is a Ritt operator for some odd positive integer $N$;
\item $T$ is a $\mathrm{Ritt}_{E}$ operator for some finite nonempty set $E\subset\mathbb T$ of roots of unity of odd order.
\end{enumerate}
The quantitative version of \textup{(ii)}$\Rightarrow$\textup{(i)} is: $\sup_n\|I-T^n\|\le2(1-\delta_X(1/(NK_+)))$, where $\delta_X$ is the modulus of convexity of $X$ and $K_+=\sup_n\|(I+T^{nN})^{-1}\|$.
<!-- end theoremb-1 -->
<!-- theoremc-1: body_md -->
Let $T$ be a Ritt operator on a Hilbert space $H$, $C=C_{\mathrm R}(T)$, $M=M(T)=\sup_{n\ge0}\|T^n\|$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every $\zeta\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$,
$\displaystyle\sup_{n\ge1}\|(\zeta-T^n)^{-1}\|\le1+\frac{CM}{|\zeta-1|}$.
\item $\displaystyle\sup_{m\ge1}C_{\mathrm R}(T^m)\le CM+2$; in particular $\sup_mC_{\mathrm R}(T^m)\leC_{\mathrm R}(T)+2$ if $T$ is a contraction.
\item If $T$ is a contraction and
$W\in A(\mathbb D;\mathcal B(E,F))$ for Hilbert spaces $E,F$, with
$\|W(1)\|<\|W\|_\infty$, then
$\sup_{n\ge1}\|W(T^n)\|<\|W\|_\infty$.
For matrix polynomials an explicit bound is given by
Theorem~\ref{thm:polydefect}. For the displacement itself,
\[
 \sup_{n\ge1}\|I-T^n\|
 \le
 \begin{cases}
  2(C+1)/(C+2),&1\le C\le\sqrt2,\\
  2\sqrt{1-C^{-2}},&C\ge\sqrt2.
 \end{cases}
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoremc-1 -->
<!-- theoremd-1: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Let $c_\infty(\mathbf n)<\infty$ and $c'\ge c_\infty(\mathbf n)$. If $T$ is power bounded, $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$, and $\sup_{k}\sup_{\eta\in\Gamma_{c'}}\|(\eta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|<\infty$, then $T$ is a Ritt operator. In particular, if $n_{k+1}/n_k\to1$, the one-point condition $\sup_k\|(\zeta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|<\infty$, for any $\zeta\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$, suffices, exactly as for the full sequence; and if $c(\mathbf n)\le c<\infty$, the norm gap $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|<2\sin\frac{\pi}{c+1}$ suffices for every power bounded operator, without a peripheral spectral assumption.
\item For $n_k=b^k$, where $b\ge2$ is an integer, the arc $\Gamma_b$ cannot be replaced by any closed arc contained in its interior, even for normal contractions with $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$; under this spectral assumption the sharp norm threshold is $\max\{1,2\sin\frac{\pi}{b+1}\}$, and without it the sharp threshold is $2\sin\frac\pi{b+1}$.
\item If $c(\mathbf n)=\infty$, then for every closed arc $\Gamma\subset\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ and every $q>1$ there are normal contractions with $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$, not Ritt, with $\sup_k\sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}\|(\eta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|<\infty$, respectively with $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|\le q$.
\item $\mathbf n$ is a Ritt sampling sequence if and only if $c(\mathbf n)<\infty$; in that case $\sup_nn\|T^n-T^{n-1}\|\le M(T)c(\mathbf n)\sup_kn_k\|T^{n_k}-T^{n_k-1}\|$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoremd-1 -->
<!-- theoreme-1: body_md -->
Fix $1<q<2$. The following assertions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every complex Banach space $X$ and every power bounded
operator $T\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$
 \sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\|I-T^n\|\le q,
 \qquad \sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}
$$
imply that $T$ is a Ritt operator.
\item The same implication holds for every normal contraction on $\ell^2$.
\item $q < \alpha(\mathcal N):= \lim_{B\to\infty}\liminf_{t\downarrow0}h_{\mathcal N}(B,t)$, where for $B,t>0$,
$$
 h_{\mathcal N}(B,t)
 :=\max\bigl\{|1-e^{int}|:n\in\mathcal N,\ nt\le B\bigr\},
$$ and the maximum of the empty set is $0$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoreme-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:BGTpowers}
If $T$ is a Ritt operator, then $\sup_{m\ge1}C_{\mathrm R}(T^m)<\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:universalPhi}
There is a nondecreasing function $F:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)$, independent of the Banach space, such that every Ritt operator satisfies
\[
 \sup_{m\ge1}C_{\mathrm R}(T^m)\le F(C_{\mathrm R}(T)).
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Clearly $M(T^m)\le M(T)$ and $\|I-T^m\|\le1+M(T)$. For $m\ge1$ and $n\ge2$, writing $I-T^m=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}T^j(I-T)$ gives
\[
 n\|T^{m(n-1)}(I-T^m)\|
 \le nD(T)\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\frac1{m(n-1)+j+1}
 \le\frac n{n-1}D(T)\le2D(T).
\]
Thus $D(T^m)\le\max\{1+M(T),2D(T)\}$. With $C=C_{\mathrm R}(T)$, \eqref{eq:quantequiv} gives the assertion with
\[
 F(C)=\max\Big\{1,\ f_2\big(f_0(C),\max\{1+f_0(C),2f_1(C)\}\big)\Big\}.
\]
The proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:boundary}
Let $S\in\mathcal B(X)$ be power bounded with $\sigma(S)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$. Then $\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}\subset\rho(S)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundary}
   C_{\mathrm R}(S)=\sup_{\xi\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}}|\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,S)\|\ \in[1,\infty].
\end{equation}
In particular $S$ is a Ritt operator if and only if the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:boundary} is finite, and then $\|R(\xi,S)\|\leC_{\mathrm R}(S)/|\xi-1|$ for $\xi\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Denote the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:boundary} (the sup) by $B$. For $\xi\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ we have $\xi\in\rho(S)$, $R(r\xi,S)\toR(\xi,S)$ in norm as $r\downarrow1$, and $|r\xi-1|\to|\xi-1|$; hence $B\leC_{\mathrm R}(S)$.

Conversely, assume $B<\infty$. We first show that $C_{\mathrm R}(S)<\infty$. Let $M=M(S)$, $z=r\xi$ with $r>1$, $\xi\in\mathbb T$. The Neumann series gives $(r-1)\|R(z,S)\|\le M$. If $\xi\ne1$, the resolvent identity $R(z,S)=R(\xi,S)+(\xi-z)R(z,S)R(\xi,S)$ gives
\[
 \|R(z,S)\|\le\|R(\xi,S)\|\bigl(1+(r-1)\|R(z,S)\|\bigr)\le(1+M)\|R(\xi,S)\|,
\]
and since $|z-1|\le(r-1)+|\xi-1|$ we obtain $|z-1|\|R(z,S)\|\le M+(1+M)B$; when $\xi=1$ the Neumann estimate alone gives $|z-1|\|R(z,S)\|\le M$. Thus $C_{\mathrm R}(S)\le M+(1+M)B<\infty$.

Consider now the operator-valued function
\[
 G(w)=(1-w)(I-wS)^{-1},\qquad w\in\mathbb D,
\]
with $G(0)=I$; for $0<|w|<1$ and $z=1/w$ one has $I-wS=w(z-S)$ and $(1-w)/w=z-1$, so that $G(w)=(z-1)R(z,S)$, and $w\mapsto z$ maps $\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$ onto $\{|z|>1\}$ and $\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ onto itself. It is holomorphic on $\mathbb D$, bounded by $C_{\mathrm R}(S)$, and extends continuously to $\overline\mathbb D\setminus\{1\}$ with $\|G(e^{it})\|\le B$ for $e^{it}\ne1$. Fix $x\in X$ and $x^*\in X^*$ of norm one and put $g(w)=\langle G(w)x,x^*\rangle$, a bounded holomorphic function on $\mathbb D$. Its radial limits $g^*(e^{it})$ exist almost everywhere and coincide with $\langle G(e^{it})x,x^*\rangle$ for $e^{it}\ne1$; the exceptional point has measure zero, so $|g^*|\le B$ almost everywhere. The Poisson representation $g(w)=\int_\mathbb T P_w\,g^*\,dm$ of bounded holomorphic functions then gives $|g(w)|\le B$ for all $w\in\mathbb D$. Taking the supremum over $x$ and $x^*$ yields $\|G(w)\|\le B$, that is, $|z-1|\|R(z,S)\|\le B$ for all $|z|>1$, and \eqref{eq:boundary} is proved. Finally $C_{\mathrm R}(S)\ge\lim_{|z|\to\infty}|z-1|\,\|R(z,S)\|=1$, so both sides of \eqref{eq:boundary} are at least $1$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
For a power bounded operator $T$ with $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\mu_N$, the same radial estimate and maximum-principle argument, now applied to $H(w)=(1-w^N)(I-wT)^{-1}$, show that $K_{\mu_N}(T)$ of Section~\ref{sec:rootsofunity} is controlled, up to a factor depending only on $N$, by the boundary supremum $\sup_{\xi\in\mathbb T\setminus\mu_N}\operatorname{dist}(\xi,\mu_N)\|R(\xi,T)\|$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:factor}
Let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$, $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ and $n\ge1$. Then
\[
  \lambda^n-T^n=(\lambda-T)\,Q_n(\lambda,T),\qquad Q_n(\lambda,T):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\lambda^{n-1-j}T^j,
\]
and the two factors commute. Consequently, if $\lambda^n\in\rho(T^n)$, then $\lambda\in\rho(T)$ and
\[
  R(\lambda,T)=Q_n(\lambda,T)\,R(\lambda^n,T^n),\qquad
  \|R(\lambda,T)\|\le M(T)\,n\max\{1,|\lambda|\}^{n-1}\,\|R(\lambda^n,T^n)\| .
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The identity is the operator form of $\lambda^n-z^n=(\lambda-z)\sum_j\lambda^{n-1-j}z^j$. If $a,b$ commute and $ab$ is invertible, then $a$ is invertible with $a^{-1}=b(ab)^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:reduction}
Let $T$ be power bounded with $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$, and suppose that for some $\delta>0$, $C>0$,
\[
   |\lambda-1|\,\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le C\qquad(|\lambda|>1,\ |\lambda-1|<\delta).
\]
Then $T$ is a Ritt operator, and $C_{\mathrm R}(T)\le\max\{3M(T),\,C,\,3B_\delta(T)\}$, where
\[
 B_\delta(T)=\sup\{\|R(\lambda,T)\|:\ 1\le|\lambda|\le2,\ |\lambda-1|\ge\delta\}<\infty.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For $|\lambda|\ge2$ the Neumann series gives $\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le M(T)/(|\lambda|-1)$ and $|\lambda-1|\le3(|\lambda|-1)$. The compact set $\{1\le|\lambda|\le2,\ |\lambda-1|\ge\delta\}$ is contained in $\rho(T)$, on which the resolvent is continuous, so $B_\delta(T)<\infty$, and $|\lambda-1|\le3$ there.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:scalarroots}
Let $N\ge1$ and $c_N:=\sin^{N-1}(\pi/N)$, with the convention $c_1=1$. For $1\le|\lambda|\le2$,
\[
   c_N\,\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mu_N)\le|\lambda^N-1|\le 3^{N-1}\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mu_N).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Write $\lambda^N-1=\prod_{\xi\in\mu_N}(\lambda-\xi)$ and let $\xi_0\in\mu_N$ be a nearest point to $\lambda$. For $\xi\ne\xi_0$, $|\lambda-\xi|\le|\lambda|+1\le3$, while $2|\lambda-\xi|\ge|\lambda-\xi|+|\lambda-\xi_0|\ge|\xi-\xi_0|\ge2\sin(\pi/N)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:TN}
Let $N\ge1$, $s_N=\sin(\pi/(2N))$, and let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\sigma(T)\subset\overline\mathbb D$.
Then $T$ is $\mathrm{Ritt}_{\mu_N}$ if and only if $T^N$ is Ritt. More precisely,
\begin{align*}
 T^N\text{ Ritt}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 M(T)\le\max_{0\le r<N}\|T^r\|M(T^N),\qquad
 K_N(T)\le \frac{M(T)C_{\mathrm R}(T^N)}{s_N},\\
 T\text{ is }\mathrm{Ritt}_{\mu_N}&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 C_{\mathrm R}(T^N)\le N K_N(T).
\end{align*}
For $N=1$ the two constants coincide.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Suppose first that $T^N$ is Ritt. Writing $n=Nk+r$ with $0\le r<N$ proves the power bound.
For $|\lambda|>1$, choose a nearest $\xi\in\mu_N$ and write
$\lambda=\xi r e^{it}$ with $r>1$ and $|t|\le\pi/N$. Then $\lambda^N-1=\lambda^N-\xi^N=(\lambda-\xi)\xi^{N-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}r^je^{ijt}$, and rotation of the sum through the angle $-(N-1)t/2$ gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}r^je^{ijt}\right|
 \ge \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}r^j\cos\bigl((j-\tfrac{N-1}{2})t\bigr)
 \ge s_N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}r^j,
\]
because $|(j-\frac{N-1}2)t|\le\frac{(N-1)\pi}{2N}=\frac\pi2-\frac{\pi}{2N}$. Consequently $|\lambda^N-1|\ge s_N\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mu_N)\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}r^j$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}, with
$\|Q_N(\lambda,T)\|\le M(T)\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}r^j$ and $\|R(\lambda^N,T^N)\|\leC_{\mathrm R}(T^N)/|\lambda^N-1|$, proves the first resolvent estimate.

Conversely, let $T$ be $\mathrm{Ritt}_{\mu_N}$, let $|\mu|>1$, let $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{N-1}$ be the $N$-th roots of $\mu$, and put $r=|\mu|^{1/N}$. The partial fraction decompositions of $1/(\mu-z^N)$ give
\[
 R(\mu,T^N)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\frac{R(\lambda_j,T)}{N\lambda_j^{N-1}}.
\]
If $\xi$ is nearest to $\lambda_j$ in $\mu_N$, then
$|\mu-1|=|\lambda_j^N-\xi^N|\le N r^{N-1}|\lambda_j-\xi|=N r^{N-1}\operatorname{dist}(\lambda_j,\mu_N)$.
Multiplying the partial fraction decomposition formula by $|\mu-1|$ and using $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda_j,\mu_N)\|R(\lambda_j,T)\|\le K_N(T)$ gives
$|\mu-1|\|R(\mu,T^N)\|\le NK_N(T)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:orbit}
Let $\lambda\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$. If $\lambda$ is not a root of unity, then $\Delta(\lambda)=2$. If $\lambda$ is a root of unity of order $m\ge2$, then $\Delta(\lambda)=2$ if $m$ is even and $\Delta(\lambda)=2\cos\frac{\pi}{2m}$ if $m$ is odd. In particular $\Delta(\lambda)\ge\sqrt3$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$, with equality exactly for $\lambda=e^{\pm2\pi i/3}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
If $\lambda$ is not a root of unity, then $\{\lambda^n\}$ is dense in $\mathbb T$ and $\Delta(\lambda)=\sup_{\eta\in\mathbb T}|\eta-1|=2$. If $\lambda$ has order $m$, then $\{\lambda^n:n\ge1\}=\mu_m$ and $\Delta(\lambda)=\max_{0\le k<m}2\sin\frac{\pi k}{m}$, which is $2$ if $m$ is even ($k=m/2$) and $2\sin\frac{\pi(m-1)}{2m}=2\cos\frac{\pi}{2m}$ if $m$ is odd. Finally $2\cos\frac\pi{2m}$ increases with $m$ and equals $\sqrt3$ for $m=3$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:sampling}
Let $\mathcal N\subset\mathbb N$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ be a closed arc. We say that $(\mathcal N,\Gamma)$ has the \emph{sampling property with constants} $(\theta_*,B)$, $\theta_*>0$, $B>0$, if for every $\theta$ with $0<|\theta|<\theta_*$ there is $n\in\mathcal N$ such that
\[
   e^{in\theta}\in\Gamma\qquad\text{and}\qquad n|\theta|\le B .
\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:master}
Let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ be power bounded, $M=M(T)$. Let $(\mathcal N,\Gamma)$ have the sampling property with constants $(\theta_*,B)$, and assume that $\Gamma\subset\rho(T^n)$ for $n\in\mathcal N$ and
\[
   K:=\sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}\|(\eta-T^n)^{-1}\|<\infty .
\]
Put $a:=\max\{1,\,B/\log(1+\tfrac1{2K})\}$, $\delta:=\min\{\theta_*/\pi,\,\tfrac12\}$ and $C:=\max\{(1+2a)M,\ 3(2K+1)MB\}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:master}
   |\lambda-1|\,\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le C\qquad(|\lambda|>1,\ |\lambda-1|<\delta).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $\lambda=re^{i\theta}$ with $r>1$, $|\theta|\le\pi$ and $|\lambda-1|<\delta$. Then $r<\frac32$, and since $|\theta|\le\frac\pi2|e^{i\theta}-1|\le\frac\pi2\big((r-1)+|\lambda-1|\big)\le\pi|\lambda-1|$, we have $|\theta|<\theta_*$.

\emph{Non-tangential region} $|\theta|\le a(r-1)$. The Neumann series gives $\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le M/(r-1)$, while $|\lambda-1|\le(r-1)+r|e^{i\theta}-1|\le(r-1)+\frac32|\theta|\le(1+2a)(r-1)$. Hence $|\lambda-1|\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le(1+2a)M$.

\emph{Tangential region} $|\theta|>a(r-1)$. In particular $\theta\ne0$, so there is $n\in\mathcal N$ with $\eta:=e^{in\theta}\in\Gamma$ and $n|\theta|\le B$. Then $n(r-1)<n|\theta|/a\le B/a$, so $r^n\le e^{n(r-1)}\le e^{B/a}\le1+\frac1{2K}$ and
\[
   |\lambda^n-\eta|=|r^ne^{in\theta}-e^{in\theta}|=r^n-1\le\frac1{2K}.
\]
Since $\lambda^n-T^n=(\eta-T^n)\big(I+(\lambda^n-\eta)(\eta-T^n)^{-1}\big)$ and $\|(\lambda^n-\eta)(\eta-T^n)^{-1}\|\le\frac12$, the operator $\lambda^n-T^n$ is invertible with $\|(\lambda^n-T^n)^{-1}\|\le2K$. Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} gives
\[
   \|R(\lambda,T)\|\le Mnr^{n-1}\cdot2K\le(2K+1)Mn .
\]
Finally $|\lambda-1|\le(r-1)+\frac32|\theta|\le(\frac1a+\frac32)|\theta|\le3|\theta|$, whence $|\lambda-1|\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le3(2K+1)M\,n|\theta|\le3(2K+1)MB$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:allpowers}
Let $\Gamma=\{e^{it}:\alpha\le t\le\gamma\}$ with $0<\alpha<\gamma<2\pi$. Then $(\mathbb N,\Gamma)$ has the sampling property with constants $(\gamma-\alpha,\,2\pi)$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $0<\theta<\gamma-\alpha$ and let $n$ be the least positive integer with $n\theta\ge\alpha$. Then $n\theta<\alpha+\theta<\gamma$, so $e^{in\theta}\in\Gamma$ and $n\theta<2\pi$. Let $-(\gamma-\alpha)<\theta<0$ and let $n$ be the least positive integer with $n|\theta|\ge2\pi-\gamma$. Then $n|\theta|<2\pi-\gamma+|\theta|<2\pi-\alpha$, so $2\pi-n|\theta|\in(\alpha,\gamma]$ and $e^{in\theta}=e^{i(2\pi-n|\theta|)}\in\Gamma$, while $n|\theta|<2\pi$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:subseq}
Let $\mathbf n=(n_k)_{k\ge0}$ be strictly increasing, let $c'>\limsup_kn_{k+1}/n_k$, and let $k_0$ be such that $n_{k+1}\le c'n_k$ for all $k\ge k_0$. Let $\Gamma=\{e^{it}:\alpha\le t\le\gamma\}$ with $0<\alpha<\gamma<2\pi$ be a closed arc such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arccond}
   \frac{\gamma}{\alpha}\ge c'\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{2\pi-\alpha}{2\pi-\gamma}\ge c' .
\end{equation}
Then $(\{n_k\},\Gamma)$ has the sampling property with constants $\big(\min\{\alpha,2\pi-\gamma\}/n_{k_0},\ \max\{\gamma,2\pi-\alpha\}\big)$. In particular this applies to $\Gamma=\Gamma_{c'}$, for which both ratios in \eqref{eq:arccond} equal $c'$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $0<\theta<\alpha/n_{k_0}$ and let $k$ be the largest index with $n_k\theta<\alpha$; it exists since $n_{k_0}\theta<\alpha$ and $n_k\to\infty$, and $k\ge k_0$. Put $n=n_{k+1}$. Then $\alpha\le n\theta\le c'n_k\theta<c'\alpha\le\gamma$, so $e^{in\theta}\in\Gamma$ and $n\theta\le\gamma$. Let $-(2\pi-\gamma)/n_{k_0}<\theta<0$ and let $k$ be the largest index with $n_k|\theta|<2\pi-\gamma$; again $k\ge k_0$, and $n=n_{k+1}$ satisfies $2\pi-\gamma\le n|\theta|<c'(2\pi-\gamma)\le2\pi-\alpha$. Hence $2\pi-n|\theta|\in(\alpha,\gamma]$, so $e^{in\theta}=e^{i(2\pi-n|\theta|)}\in\Gamma$, and $n|\theta|\le2\pi-\alpha$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:general}
Let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ be power bounded with $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$. Let $(\mathcal N,\Gamma)$ have the sampling property and assume that
\[
   \sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}\|(\eta-T^n)^{-1}\|<\infty .
\]
Then $T$ is a Ritt operator.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:kato}
Let $T$ be power bounded with $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$, and let $\zeta\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ with $K_\zeta:=\sup_{n\ge1}\|(\zeta-T^n)^{-1}\|<\infty$. Then $T$ is a Ritt operator.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $\varepsilon:=\frac12\min\{1/(2K_\zeta),|\zeta-1|\}$ and $\Gamma:=\{\eta\in\mathbb T:|\eta-\zeta|\le\varepsilon\}$, a closed arc in $\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$. For $\eta\in\Gamma$ and $n\ge1$, the Neumann series gives $\eta\in\rho(T^n)$ and $\|(\eta-T^n)^{-1}\|\le\frac43K_\zeta\le2K_\zeta$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:allpowers} and Proposition~\ref{thm:general}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:dependT}
The local estimate \eqref{eq:master} is uniform, but Proposition~\ref{thm:general} and Corollary~\ref{cor:kato} do not bound $C_{\mathrm R}(T)$ in terms of upper bounds on $M(T)$ and $K_\zeta$ and the point $\zeta$ alone. Indeed, let $\zeta\in\mathbb T\setminus\mu_3$ and $T_\rho=\rho\omegaI$ on $\mathbb C$, where $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and $0<\rho<1$. Then $M(T_\rho)=1$ and $\sigma(T_\rho)\cap\mathbb T=\emptyset$. For $\zeta,\xi\in\mathbb T$ and $0\le r\le1$,
\[
 |\zeta-\xi|\le|\zeta-r\xi|+(1-r)\le2|\zeta-r\xi|,
\]
because $|\zeta-r\xi|\ge1-r$. Taking $\xi=\omega^n$ and $r=\rho^n$ gives
\[
 K_\zeta(T_\rho):=\sup_n|\zeta-\rho^n\omega^n|^{-1}
 \le\frac2{\operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\mu_3)}
 \qquad(0<\rho<1).
\]
On the other hand,
$C_{\mathrm R}(T_\rho)\ge\lim_{r\downarrow1}|r\omega-1|/(r-\rho)=\sqrt3/(1-\rho)\to\infty$ as $\rho\uparrow1$. This explains the operator-dependent constant $B_\delta(T)$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:reduction}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:divdiff}
Let $S\in\mathcal B(X)$ be power bounded, $w\in A^{1,1}(\mathbb D)$, and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb T$ be a closed arc with $\|w(S)\|<m_{\Gamma}(w)$. Then $\Gamma\subset\rho(S)$ and
\[
   \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}\|(\eta-S)^{-1}\|\le\frac{M(S)\|w\|_{A^{1,1}}}{m_{\Gamma}(w)-\|w(S)\|}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We give a short proof for completeness. For $\eta\in\mathbb T$ let $h_\eta(z)=(w(\eta)-w(z))/(\eta-z)=\sum_{k\ge1}c_k\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}\eta^{k-1-r}z^r$. The series converges absolutely after evaluation at $S$, with $\|h_\eta(S)\|\le M(S)\sum_{k\ge1}k|c_k|\le M(S)\|w\|_{A^{1,1}}$. The identity $w(\eta)-w(S)=(\eta-S)h_\eta(S)$ holds with commuting factors. If $\eta\in\Gamma$, the left-hand side is invertible with inverse of norm at most $(m_{\Gamma}(w)-\|w(S)\|)^{-1}$, so $\eta-S$ is invertible and $(\eta-S)^{-1}=h_\eta(S)(w(\eta)-w(S))^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:defect}
Let $T$ be power bounded with $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$, let $(\mathcal N,\Gamma)$ have the sampling property, and let $w\in A^{1,1}(\mathbb D)$ satisfy $\sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\|w(T^n)\|<m_{\Gamma}(w)$. Then $T$ is a Ritt operator.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:divdiff} to $S=T^n$, $n\in\mathcal N$; note that $M(T^n)\le M(T)$. Then apply Proposition~\ref{thm:general}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:local}
Let $T$ satisfy \eqref{eq:q}. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset E_q$;
\item there are $\delta(q)>0$ and $C(q)<\infty$, depending only on $q$, such that
\[
   |\lambda-1|\,\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le C(q)\qquad(|\lambda|>1,\ |\lambda-1|<\delta(q));
\]
one may take, with $t_q:=2\arcsin\frac{q+2}4\in(0,\pi)$ and $a_q:=\max\{1,\,2\pi/\log(1+\frac{2-q}4)\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:localconstants}
   \delta(q)=\min\Big\{2-\frac{2t_q}\pi,\ \frac12\Big\},\qquad
   C(q)=\max\Big\{(1+2a_q)(1+q),\ \frac{6\pi(1+q)(6-q)}{2-q}\Big\};
\end{equation}
these functions are respectively nonincreasing and nondecreasing in $q$;
\item $T$ is a Ritt operator if and only if $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(i) If $\lambda\in\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T$, then $1-\lambda^n\in\sigma(I-T^n)$ and $|1-\lambda^n|\le\|I-T^n\|\le q$ for all $n$, i.e.\ $\Delta(\lambda)\le q$.

(ii) Fix $a:=(q+2)/2\in(q,2)$ and let $\Gamma:=\{\eta\in\mathbb T:|\eta-1|\ge a\}=\{e^{it}:t_q\le t\le2\pi-t_q\}$, since $|e^{it}-1|=2\sin(t/2)\ge a$ exactly when $t_q\le t\le2\pi-t_q$. For $\eta\in\Gamma$,
$\eta-T^n=(\eta-1)I+(I-T^n)$ with $\|I-T^n\|\le q<a\le|\eta-1|$, so the Neumann series gives
$\Gamma\subset\rho(T^n)$ and
$\|(\eta-T^n)^{-1}\|\le(a-q)^{-1}=2/(2-q)=:K$, uniformly in $n$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:allpowers}, $(\mathbb N,\Gamma)$ has the sampling property with constants $(2\pi-2t_q,2\pi)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:master} with $M=1+q$, $B=2\pi$ and $\frac1{2K}=\frac{2-q}4$ gives the estimate with $\delta=\min\{(2\pi-2t_q)/\pi,\frac12\}$ and $C=\max\{(1+2a_q)(1+q),3(2K+1)(1+q)2\pi\}$, where $2K+1=(6-q)/(2-q)$; this is \eqref{eq:localconstants}. As $q$ increases, $t_q$, $K$ and $a_q$ increase, so $\delta(q)$ decreases and $C(q)$ increases.

(iii) Ritt operators satisfy $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$. Conversely, Lemma~\ref{lem:reduction} applies.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:uniformescape}
Let $1\le q<2$ and $\varepsilon>0$. There are $a=a(q,\varepsilon)>q$, $n_0=n_0(q,\varepsilon)\in\mathbb N$ and $\kappa=\kappa(q,\varepsilon)>0$ such that for every $\lambda=re^{i\theta}$ with $1<r\le1+\kappa$ and $\operatorname{dist}(e^{i\theta},E_q)\ge\varepsilon$ there is $n\le n_0$ with $|\lambda^n-1|\ge a$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The set $F:=\{\eta\in\mathbb T:\operatorname{dist}(\eta,E_q)\ge\varepsilon\}$ is compact. If $F$ is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, note that $\Delta=\sup_n|\eta^n-1|$ is lower semicontinuous on $\mathbb T$ as a supremum of continuous functions. Since $F\cap E_q=\emptyset$, $\Delta>q$ on $F$, so $a':=\min_F\Delta>q$. Put $a_1:=(q+a')/2$. For each $\eta\in F$ choose $n(\eta)$ with $|\eta^{n(\eta)}-1|>a_1$; the sets $\{\eta':|\eta'^{\,n(\eta)}-1|>a_1\}$ are open and cover $F$, so finitely many suffice, and we let $n_0$ be the largest of the corresponding $n(\eta)$. Choose $\kappa>0$ with $(1+\kappa)^{n_0}-1\le(a_1-q)/2$ and put $a:=(a_1+q)/2$. If $\lambda=re^{i\theta}$ with $1<r\le1+\kappa$ and $e^{i\theta}\in F$, pick $n\le n_0$ with $|e^{in\theta}-1|>a_1$; then $|\lambda^n-e^{in\theta}|=r^n-1\le(a_1-q)/2$, so $|\lambda^n-1|\ge a$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:oddN}
Let $T$ satisfy \eqref{eq:q}, $1\le q<2$, and let $N=N(q)$. Then $T$ is a $\mathrm{Ritt}_{E_q}$ operator and $T^N$ is a Ritt operator, with
\[
   K_{E_q}(T)\le\Phi(q),\qquad C_{\mathrm R}(T^N)\le N\Phi(q),
\]
where $\Phi(q)$ depends only on $q$. In particular, if $\sup_n\|I-T^n\|<2$, then $T^N$ is a Ritt operator for some odd $N$; equivalently, $T$ is a $\mathrm{Ritt}_{E}$ operator for a finite nonempty set $E$ of roots of unity of odd order.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Put $M:=1+q\ge M(T)$ and $S:=T^N$. Since $E_q\subset\mu_N$, Theorem~\ref{thm:local}(i) and the spectral mapping theorem give $\sigma(S)\cap\mathbb T=\{\lambda^N:\lambda\in\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\}\subset\{1\}$, and $\sup_n\|I-S^n\|\le q$. Let $\delta_0=\delta(q)$, $C_0=C(q)$ be the constants of Theorem~\ref{thm:local}(ii) applied to $S$.

\emph{Step 1: estimates near $E_q$.} Put $\delta_1:=\min\{\delta_0/(N2^{N-1}),\ \sin(\pi/N)\}$ if $N\ge2$ and $\delta_1:=\min\{\delta_0/(N2^{N-1}),\ 1\}$ if $N=1$. Let $\xi\in E_q$ and $|\lambda|>1$ with $|\lambda-\xi|<\delta_1$; write $\lambda=\xi w$, so $|w|>1$, $|w-1|<\delta_1\le1$, $|w|<2$ and $\lambda^N=w^N$. Since $|w^N-1|=|w-1|\,|\sum_{j<N}w^j|\le N2^{N-1}|w-1|<\delta_0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:local}(ii) for $S$ gives $\|R(\lambda^N,S)\|\le C_0/|\lambda^N-1|$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}, $\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le MN2^{N-1}C_0/|\lambda^N-1|$. For $N\ge2$, the inequalities $|\lambda-\xi|<\sin(\pi/N)$ and $|\xi-\eta|\ge2\sin(\pi/N)$ for distinct $\xi,\eta\in\mu_N$ show that $\xi$ is the nearest point of $\mu_N$ to $\lambda$; for $N=1$ this is automatic. Lemma~\ref{lem:scalarroots} therefore gives $|\lambda^N-1|\ge c_N|\lambda-\xi|$. Hence
\[
   \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_q)\,\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le|\lambda-\xi|\,\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le C_1:=\frac{MN2^{N-1}C_0}{c_N}.
\]

\emph{Step 2: estimates away from $E_q$.} Let $a,n_0,\kappa$ be given by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformescape} with $\varepsilon=\delta_1/2$, and assume also $\kappa\le\delta_1/2$. Let $\lambda=re^{i\theta}$, $|\lambda|>1$, $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_q)\ge\delta_1$. If $r\ge1+\kappa$, the Neumann series gives $\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le M/(r-1)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_q)\le r+1\le\frac{2+\kappa}{\kappa}(r-1)$. If $1<r<1+\kappa$, then $\operatorname{dist}(e^{i\theta},E_q)\ge\delta_1-(r-1)\ge\delta_1/2$, so there is $n\le n_0$ with $|\lambda^n-1|\ge a>q$. Since $\|I-T^n\|\le q$, the operator $\lambda^n-T^n=(\lambda^n-1)I+(I-T^n)$ is invertible with $\|(\lambda^n-T^n)^{-1}\|\le(a-q)^{-1}$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} gives $\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le Mn_02^{n_0}/(a-q)$, while $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_q)\le3$.

Together, $K_{E_q}(T)\le\Phi(q):=\max\{C_1,\ M(2+\kappa)/\kappa,\ 3Mn_02^{n_0}/(a-q)\}$, which depends only on $q$. Since $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mu_N)\le\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_q)$, also $K_N(T)\le\Phi(q)$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:TN} shows that $T^N$ is Ritt with $C_{\mathrm R}(T^N)\le N\Phi(q)$.

For the last assertion: if $T^N$ is Ritt with $N$ odd, then $T$ is $\mathrm{Ritt}_{\mu_N}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:TN}, and $\mu_N$ consists of roots of unity of odd order; conversely, if $T$ is $\mathrm{Ritt}_{E}$ with $E$ a finite nonempty set of roots of unity of odd order and $N$ is the least common multiple of their orders, then $N$ is odd, $E\subset\mu_N$, $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mu_N)\le\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)$, so $T$ is $\mathrm{Ritt}_{\mu_N}$ and $T^N$ is Ritt by Proposition~\ref{prop:TN}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remarks-1: body_md -->
(a) Theorem~\ref{thm:oddN} shows that the spectral hypothesis $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$ in the discrete zero--two law \cite[Corollary~6.1]{BGT} is exactly the hypothesis that excludes the finitely many odd-order roots of unity in $E_q$; for $q<\sqrt3$ it is automatic (Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt3}).

(b) The only non-explicit step in the proof is the compactness argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformescape}; all the other constants are explicit. For $q<\sqrt3$ the compactness can be replaced by an explicit hitting argument, which gives a reciprocal bound (Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt3}); the sharp leading constant is determined in Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-asymptotic}.

(c) The parity restriction concerns the converse (Theorem~\ref{thm:UCchar}) only: $T=-I$ has $T^2=I$ Ritt while $\|I-T\|=2$. In the forward implication every multiple of $N(q)$, even ones included, is an admissible exponent, as the next proposition shows.
<!-- end remarks-1 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:minimalexponent}
Fix $1\le q<2$ and $L\ge1$. The implication
\[
 \sup_{n\ge1}\|I-T^n\|\le q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T^L\text{ is Ritt}
\]
holds for every bounded operator on every complex Banach space if and only if
$N(q)$ divides $L$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
If $L$ is a multiple of $N(q)$, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:oddN} and the stability
of the Ritt property under positive integer powers (Theorem~\ref{thm:BGTpowers}). Conversely, for each
$\xi\in E_q$, apply the asserted implication to the scalar operator $T=\xi$, which satisfies \eqref{eq:q} by definition of $E_q$.
A unimodular scalar is Ritt only when it is $1$, so $\xi^L=1$. Thus every
order occurring in $E_q$ divides $L$, and so does their least common multiple.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:cubic}
Let $\sqrt3\le q<2\cos\frac{\pi}{10}\approx1.902$ and $\sup_n\|I-T^n\|\le q$. Then $T^3$ is a Ritt operator, $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\mu_3$, and $\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le\Phi(q)/\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mu_3)$ for $|\lambda|>1$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:sqrt3}
Let $1\le q<\sqrt3$ and $\sup_{n\ge1}\|I-T^n\|\le q$. Then $T$ is a Ritt operator and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rate}
 C_{\mathrm R}(T)\le\frac{2\sqrt3 M(T)}{\sqrt3-q}
          \le\frac{6+2\sqrt3}{\sqrt3-q}.
\end{equation}
For $0\le r<1$, put
\[
 a_r=r\exp\bigl(i\arccos(-r/2)\bigr).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qrho}
 q_r:=\sup_{n\ge1}|1-a_r^n|=\sqrt{1+2r^2},
 \qquad
 C_{\mathrm R}(a_r)=\frac{2q_r}{1-r^2}=\frac{4q_r}{3-q_r^2}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-scalar-lower}
 \frac{4q}{3-q^2}\le\Phi_*(q)
             \le\frac{6+2\sqrt3}{\sqrt3-q}
 \qquad(1\le q<\sqrt3).
\end{equation}
The threshold $\sqrt3$ is optimal: $T=e^{2\pi i/3}I$ satisfies
$\sup_n\|I-T^n\|=\sqrt3$ and is not Ritt. For every $q\in[\sqrt3,2)$, the Ritt constants of operators satisfying $\sup_n\|I-T^n\|\le q$ are unbounded, even for scalar operators with spectrum in $\mathbb D$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:explicitescape}
For every $\xi\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that
\[
 |\xi^n-1|\ge\sqrt3,
 \qquad n|\xi-1|\le2\sqrt3.
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Write $\xi=e^{i\theta}$ with $0<|\theta|\le\pi$. If $|\theta|\ge2\pi/3$, take $n=1$. Otherwise take $n=\lceil2\pi/(3|\theta|)\rceil$. Then
\[
 \frac{2\pi}3\le n|\theta|<\frac{2\pi}3+|\theta|<\frac{4\pi}3,
\]
so $|\xi^n-1|\ge\sqrt3$. If $n=2$, then
$n|\xi-1|=4\sin(|\theta|/2)\le2\sqrt3$. If $n\ge3$, the minimality of $n$ gives
\[
 n|\xi-1|\le n|\theta|<\frac{2\pi n}{3(n-1)}\le\pi<2\sqrt3.
\]
For $n=1$, use $|\xi-1|\le2$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The spectral mapping theorem and Lemma~\ref{lem:orbit} give
$\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$, while $M(T)\le1+q$. For
$\xi\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$, choose $n$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:explicitescape}. The identity
\[
 \xi^n-T^n=(\xi^n-1)I+(I-T^n)
\]
and the Neumann series give
$\|R(\xi^n,T^n)\|\le(\sqrt3-q)^{-1}$. Hence Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} yields
\[
 |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|
 \le\frac{M(T)n|\xi-1|}{\sqrt3-q}
 \le\frac{2\sqrt3 M(T)}{\sqrt3-q}.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary} proves \eqref{eq:rate}.

For the scalar assertions, note that $|a_r|=r$ and
$a_r+\bar a_r=-r^2$. Thus
\[
 |1+a_r|=1,
 \qquad a_r^2+r^2a_r+r^2=0,
 \qquad a_r^{n+3}=r^2a_r^n+(1-r^2)a_r^{n+2}\quad(n\ge0).
\]
The last identity follows by multiplying the quadratic identity by
$a_r-1$ and then by $a_r^n$. Its coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one. Induction therefore shows that every power of $a_r$ belongs to
$\operatorname{conv}\{1,a_r,a_r^2\}$. Moreover,
\[
 |1-a_r|^2=1+2r^2,
 \qquad |1-a_r^2|=|1-a_r|\,|1+a_r|=|1-a_r|.
\]
Convexity of $z\mapsto|1-z|$ proves the first identity in \eqref{eq:qrho}.

For every $a\in\mathbb D$, the substitution $w=1/\lambda$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-ritt-exact}
 C_{\mathrm R}(a)=\sup_{|w|<1}\left|\frac{1-w}{1-aw}\right|
        =\frac{2|1-a|}{1-|a|^2}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the displayed M\"obius map has image the disc with centre
$(1-\bar a)/(1-|a|^2)$ and radius $|1-a|/(1-|a|^2)$; the modulus of the centre equals the radius. Applying this formula to $a_r$ proves the remaining identities in \eqref{eq:qrho}. Since $r\mapsto q_r$ maps $[0,1)$ onto $[1,\sqrt3)$, it also proves \eqref{eq:sharp-scalar-lower}. As $r\uparrow1$, the operators $a_r$ have unbounded Ritt constants and displacement bounds below $\sqrt3$. Finally, the orbit of $e^{2\pi i/3}$ has displacement $\sqrt3$, and this scalar operator has a peripheral spectral point different from $1$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:sharp-asymptotic}
As $q\uparrow\sqrt3$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-asymptotic}
 \Phi_*(q)=\frac{2}{\sqrt3-q}+O(1).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
 \lim_{q\uparrow\sqrt3}(\sqrt3-q)\Phi_*(q)=2.
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The lower bound follows from \eqref{eq:sharp-scalar-lower}, since
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lower-asymptotic}
 \frac{4q}{3-q^2}
 =\frac{2}{\sqrt3-q}-\frac1{\sqrt3}+O(\sqrt3-q).
\end{equation}
For the upper bound, let $\varepsilon=\sqrt3-q$,
$M_0=1+\sqrt3$, and suppose
$\sup_n\|I-T^n\|\le q$. Then $M(T)\le M_0$. All constants below are independent of $T$, $X$ and $\varepsilon$.

Put $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and define
\[
 p(z)=\frac23e^{i\pi/6}(1-z)
             +\frac13e^{-i\pi/6}(1-z^2).
\]
The displacement bounds for the first two powers give $\|p(T)\|\le q$. Direct calculation yields
\[
 p(\omega)=\sqrt3,
 \qquad p'(\omega)=-\frac1{\sqrt3}-i,
 \qquad |p'(\omega)|=\frac2{\sqrt3},
 \qquad \operatorname{Re}\bigl(i\omega p'(\omega)\bigr)=0.
\]
Write $\xi(\delta)=\omega e^{i\delta}$. The last identity says that the derivative of $|p(\xi(\delta))|$ at $\delta=0$ vanishes. Taylor's theorem therefore gives constants $A>0$ and $\delta_0>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-contact}
 |p(\xi(\delta))|\ge\sqrt3-A\delta^2,
 \qquad
 |\xi(\delta)-1|\,|p'(\xi(\delta))|\le2+A|\delta|
 \quad(|\delta|\le\delta_0).
\end{equation}
The two roots of $p(z)=p(\xi)$ are $\xi$ and
\[
 \eta=-2e^{i\pi/3}-\xi.
\]
At $\xi=\omega$ the second root has modulus $\sqrt7$.
By decreasing $\delta_0$, we may assume $|\eta|\ge2$ whenever
$|\delta|\le\delta_0$. Thus $\eta\in\rho(T)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:second-root-bound}
 \|R(\eta,T)\|\le\frac{M(T)}{|\eta|-1}\le M_0.
\end{equation}
Whenever $|p(\xi)|>q$, the partial fraction decomposition give the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadratic-resolvent}
 R(\xi,T)
 =p'(\xi)\bigl(p(\xi)I-p(T)\bigr)^{-1}
       +R(\eta,T).
\end{equation}
To verify it, write $p(z)=az^2+bz+c$, where
$a=-e^{-i\pi/6}/3$. Then
$p(\xi)-p(z)=-a(\xi-z)(\eta-z)$ and
$p'(\xi)=a(\xi-\eta)$, which give
$p'(\xi)/(p(\xi)-p(z))=(\xi-z)^{-1}-(\eta-z)^{-1}$.

Fix $K\ge1$ for the moment. For $|\delta|\le K\varepsilon$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, depending only on $K$, equations
\eqref{eq:quadratic-contact}--\eqref{eq:quadratic-resolvent} imply
\begin{align*}
 |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|
 &\le\frac{2+AK\varepsilon}
              {\varepsilon-AK^2\varepsilon^2}+2M_0\\
 &\le\frac2\varepsilon+C_K.
\end{align*}
Here $C_K$ is finite and independent of $T$ and $\varepsilon$; the second inequality follows, for example, by requiring
$AK^2\varepsilon\le1/2$ and expanding $(1-AK^2\varepsilon)^{-1}$.

We next control the rest of the fixed arc around $\omega$. After decreasing $\delta_0$ again, there is $c>0$ such that
\[
 |1-\xi(\delta)|\ge\sqrt3+c\delta
       \quad(0\le\delta\le\delta_0),
 \qquad
 |1-\xi(\delta)^2|\ge\sqrt3+c|\delta|
       \quad(-\delta_0\le\delta\le0).
\]
Indeed, the relevant functions are
$2\sin(\pi/3+\delta/2)$ and $2\sin(2\pi/3+\delta)$, whose derivatives at zero are $1/2$ and $-1$, respectively. Applying the Neumann series to the first power in the first case and to the second power in the second case, and then using Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}, gives
\[
 |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|
 \le\frac{4M_0}{\varepsilon+c|\delta|}
       \quad(|\delta|\le\delta_0).
\]
Choose $K$ once and for all so that $4M_0/(1+cK)\le1$. Then the last bound is at most $1/\varepsilon$ whenever
$K\varepsilon\le|\delta|\le\delta_0$. Together with the previous estimate, this proves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-arc-bound}
 |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|\le\frac2\varepsilon+C
\end{equation}
on a fixed arc about $\omega$, with an absolute $C$. The polynomial
$\widetilde p(z)=\overline{p(\bar z)}$ gives the same bound on a fixed arc about $\bar\omega$.

To complete the proof, observe that the remaining part of the circle has a uniform bound independent of $\varepsilon$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:local}(ii) with displacement bound $\sqrt3$. Taking radial limits in that estimate gives
\[
 |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|\le C(\sqrt3)
 \quad\bigl(0<|\xi-1|<\delta(\sqrt3)/2\bigr).
\]
Choose disjoint open arcs about $1$, $\omega$ and $\bar\omega$, with closures contained in the regions already controlled, and let $H$ be their complement in $\mathbb T$. Every $\zeta\in H$ has
$\Delta(\zeta)>\sqrt3$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:orbit}. For each such $\zeta$, choose an integer $n(\zeta)$ and an open neighbourhood on which
$|1-\xi^{n(\zeta)}|>\sqrt3$. Finitely many of these neighbourhoods cover the compact set $H$. If $N$ is the largest of the corresponding exponents, continuity gives
\[
 g:=\min_{\xi\in H}\max_{1\le n\le N}|1-\xi^n|>\sqrt3.
\]
The Neumann series and Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} now give
\[
 |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|
 \le\frac{2M_0N}{g-\sqrt3}
 \qquad(\xi\in H).
\]
Combining this estimate with \eqref{eq:critical-arc-bound} and the estimate near $1$, and taking $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, proves
\[
 \sup_{\xi\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}}
       |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|
 \le\frac2\varepsilon+C'
\]
with an absolute $C'$. Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary} and
\eqref{eq:lower-asymptotic} complete the proof.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:higher-thresholds}
Let $m\ge3$ be odd, $Q=Q_m$, and $Q_m^-\le q<Q$. Every operator satisfying
$\sup_{n\ge1}\|I-T^n\|\le q$ obeys
\begin{equation}\label{eq:higher-threshold-bound}
 K_{E_q}(T)\le\frac{6m(1+Q)\Phi(Q)}{Q-q},
\end{equation}
where $\Phi$ is the uniform bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:oddN}. Moreover, there are constants $c_m>0$ and $\varepsilon_m>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:higher-threshold-lower}
 \sup\left\{K_{E_q}(a):\ a\in\mathbb D,\
                  \sup_{n\ge1}|1-a^n|\le q\right\}
 \ge\frac{c_m}{Q-q}
 \qquad(Q-\varepsilon_m<q<Q).
\end{equation}
Thus the reciprocal order in \eqref{eq:higher-threshold-bound} is sharp at every threshold.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Put $E=E_m^-$, $F=E_Q$, $\varepsilon=Q-q$ and $M=1+q$. Theorem~\ref{thm:oddN}, applied at the bound $Q$, gives
$K_F(T)\le\Phi(Q)$. For each $\xi\in F\setminus E$, the orbit of $\xi$ contains a point at distance $Q$ from $1$, so there is $1\le n\le m$ with $|1-\xi^n|=Q$. The Neumann series and Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} imply
\[
 \xi\in\rho(T),\qquad
 \|R(\xi,T)\|\le\frac{nM}{\varepsilon}
                         \le\frac{mM}{\varepsilon}.
\]
Let $h=\varepsilon/(2mM)$. If $|\lambda-\xi|\le h$, resolvent perturbation gives
\[
 \|R(\lambda,T)\|\le\frac{2mM}{\varepsilon}.
\]
Since $E$ is nonempty, $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\le h+2\le3$ on each of these balls. Hence
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\,\|R(\lambda,T)\|
 \le\frac{6mM}{\varepsilon}
\]
there. Outside their union, if a nearest point of $F$ to $\lambda$ belongs to $E$, then
$\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)=\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,F)$. Otherwise,
$\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,F)\ge h$, and comparison with any point of $E$ gives
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\le\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,F)+2
      \le(1+2/h)\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,F).
\]
Because $\varepsilon<1$ and $mM\ge1$,
$1+2/h\le6mM/\varepsilon$. Thus, for all $|\lambda|>1$ outside the balls,
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\,\|R(\lambda,T)\|
 \le\frac{6mM\Phi(Q)}{\varepsilon}.
\]
The constant $\Phi(Q)$ is at least $1$, as follows by letting $|\lambda|\to\infty$ in the defining resolvent bound. Using $M\le1+Q$ proves \eqref{eq:higher-threshold-bound}.

For the lower bound, fix a root $\xi$ of exact order $m$ and let $a_r=r\xi$, where $r<1$ tends to $1$. For $1\le j\le m$, set
$f_j(r)=|1-r^j\xi^j|$. If $n\equiv j\pmod m$ and $n\ge j$, then $r^n\xi^j$ lies on the segment joining $0$ to $r^j\xi^j$; hence
$|1-r^n\xi^j|\le\max\{1,f_j(r)\}$. Since $a_r^n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, this proves
\[
 q(r):=\sup_{n\ge1}|1-a_r^n|
      =\max\{1,f_1(r),\ldots,f_m(r)\}.
\]
At $r=1$, precisely two indices $j_1,j_2\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}$ satisfy $f_j(1)=Q$; they obey $j_1+j_2=m$. All other values are strictly smaller than $Q$. For either of these two indices,
\[
 f_j'(1)=\frac{j(1-\operatorname{Re}\xi^j)}{|1-\xi^j|}
             =\frac{jQ}{2}.
\]
Consequently, with $j_*:=\min\{j_1,j_2\}$, for all $r<1$ sufficiently close to $1$ one has $q(r)=f_{j_*}(r)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:higher-scalar-asymptotic}
 Q-q(r)=\frac{j_*Q}{2}(1-r)+O((1-r)^2).
\end{equation}
In particular, $q(r)<Q$ and $q(r)$ is strictly increasing on an interval ending at $1$, so every $q$ sufficiently close to $Q$ from below equals some $q(r)$.
Put $d=\operatorname{dist}(\xi,E)>0$. By approaching $\xi$ radially from outside the unit disc,
\[
 K_E(a_r)\ge\frac{d}{1-r}.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:higher-scalar-asymptotic}, this gives
\[
 \liminf_{r\uparrow1}(Q-q(r))K_E(a_r)
       \ge\frac{dj_*Q}{2}>0,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:higher-threshold-lower}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:generalsymbolstructure}
Let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ be power bounded, let $w\in A^{1,1}(\mathbb D)$, and suppose that
\[
   \sup_{n\ge1}\|w(T^n)\|\le q<\|w\|_\infty.
\]
Define
\[
   E=E(w,q):=\Big\{\lambda\in\mathbb T:
                  \sup_{n\ge1}|w(\lambda^n)|\le q\Big\}.
\]
Then $E$ is a finite set of roots of unity and
$\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset E$. More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $E=\emptyset$, then $r(T)<1$.
\item If $E\ne\emptyset$, then $1\in E$. If $N$ is the least common
multiple of the orders of the elements of $E$, then $T^N$ is a Ritt
operator and $T$ is a $\mathrm{Ritt}_{E}$ operator.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
If $\lambda\in\mathbb T$ is not a root of unity, its positive powers are dense
in $\mathbb T$, so continuity gives
$\sup_{n\ge1}|w(\lambda^n)|=\|w\|_\infty>q$. If $\lambda$ has order $m$,
then
\[
   \sup_{n\ge1}|w(\lambda^n)|=\max_{\eta\in\mu_m}|w(\eta)|.
\]
Uniform continuity of $w$ on $\mathbb T$ shows that the right-hand side tends
to $\|w\|_\infty$ as $m\to\infty$. Thus the orders occurring in $E$
are bounded, and $E$ is finite. If $E$ contains an element of order $m$,
then $|w(1)|=|w(\lambda^m)|\le q$, whence $1\in E$.

For the peripheral spectrum inclusion, let $\lambda\in\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T$
and fix $n\ge1$. The spectral mapping theorem gives
$\eta:=\lambda^n\in\sigma(T^n)\cap\mathbb T$. The divided-difference identity
from Lemma~\ref{lem:divdiff}, with $S=T^n$, is
\[
   w(\eta)I-w(S)=(\etaI-S)h_\eta(S).
\]
The series defining $h_\eta(S)$ converges in operator norm because
$w\in A^{1,1}(\mathbb D)$ and $S$ is power bounded. The two factors on the
right commute. If their product were invertible, then
$\etaI-S$ would also be invertible, a contradiction. Consequently
\[
   w(\lambda^n)\in\sigma(w(T^n)),\qquad
   |w(\lambda^n)|\le\|w(T^n)\|\le q.
\]
Since $n$ was arbitrary, $\lambda\in E$. If $E=\emptyset$, compactness
of $\sigma(T)\subset\overline\mathbb D$ gives $r(T)<1$.

Suppose that $E\ne\emptyset$, and put $S=T^N$. Then $S$ is
power bounded and 
\[
   \sigma(S)\cap\mathbb T
      =\{\lambda^N:\lambda\in\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\}
      \subset\{1\},
   \qquad
   \sup_{n\ge1}\|w(S^n)\|\le q.
\]
Since $|w(1)|\le q<\|w\|_\infty$, there is a closed arc
$\Gamma\subset\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ of positive length such that
$m_\Gamma(w)>q$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:allpowers}, $(\mathbb N,\Gamma)$ has the
sampling property. Corollary~\ref{cor:defect} shows that $S$
is Ritt, and Proposition~\ref{prop:TN} shows that $T$ is
$\mathrm{Ritt}_{\mu_N}$.

To remove the points of $\mu_N\setminus E$, choose $0<\delta<1$
smaller than half the distance between distinct points of $\mu_N$
when $N>1$; for $N=1$ choose any $\delta\in(0,1)$. If
$|\lambda|>1$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)<\delta$, a nearest point of
$\mu_N$ belongs to $E$, and hence
\[
   \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\|R(\lambda,T)\|
      =\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mu_N)\|R(\lambda,T)\|
      \le K_N(T).
\]
The compact set
\[
   \{\lambda:1\le|\lambda|\le2,
                   \ \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\ge\delta\}
\]
is disjoint from $\sigma(T)$, so the resolvent is bounded there.
For $|\lambda|\ge2$, using the power-boundedness of $T$ the Neumann series gives
\[
   \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\|R(\lambda,T)\|
      \le\frac{(|\lambda|+1)M(T)}{|\lambda|-1}
      \le3M(T).
\]
Thus $K_E(T)<\infty$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:symbol-constructive}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:generalsymbolstructure}, suppose
that $E=E(w,q)\ne\emptyset$, and put $M=M(T)$ and
$D=\max_{\xi\in E}\operatorname{ord}(\xi)$. Choose a closed arc
$\Gamma\subset\mathbb T$ of angular length $\ell>0$ and a number $a>q$ such that
\[
   \min_{\eta\in\Gamma}|w(\eta)|\ge a.
\]
Let $U$ be the union of the open angular neighbourhoods of radius
$\ell/(2D)$ about the points of $E$, and set $F_0=\mathbb T\setminus U$.
If $F_0\ne\emptyset$, there exists $N\ge1$ such that
\[
   g:=\min_{\eta\in F_0}\max_{1\le n\le N}|w(\eta^n)|-q>0.
\]
For any such $N$ and $g$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symbol-constructive}
   K_E(T)\le M+(1+M)ML_w
      \max\left\{\frac{2\pi}{a-q},\frac{2N}{g}\right\}.
\end{equation}
When $F_0=\emptyset$, the second term in the maximum is omitted.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Since $1\in E$, we have $|w(1)|\le q$, so $1\notin\Gamma$ and
$0<\ell<2\pi$. In particular the angular neighbourhoods used above
have radius less than $\pi$. Every point $\eta\in F_0$ lies outside
$E$, and therefore $|w(\eta^n)|>q$ for some $n\ge1$. The corresponding
open sets cover $F_0$. Compactness gives a finite subcover and hence
an integer $N$ for which the continuous function
$\max_{1\le n\le N}|w(\eta^n)|$ is everywhere greater than $q$ on
$F_0$. Its minimum exceeds $q$, proving the existence of $g$.

For any $n\ge1$, apply the divided-difference argument directly to
$v_n(z)=w(z^n)$. Its weighted coefficient sum is $nL_w$, and
$v_n(T)=w(T^n)$. Consequently, whenever $\eta\in\mathbb T$ and
$|w(\eta^n)|>q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symbol-direct-divdiff}
   \|R(\eta,T)\|
      \le\frac{MnL_w}{|w(\eta^n)|-q}.
\end{equation}
For $\eta\in F_0$, choose a witnessing $n\le N$. Since
$\operatorname{dist}(\eta,E)\le2$, this gives
\[
   \operatorname{dist}(\eta,E)\|R(\eta,T)\|
      \le\frac{2MNL_w}{g}.
\]

Now let $\eta\in U\setminus E$. Choose $\xi\in E$ and write
$\eta=\xi e^{it}$ with $0<|t|<\ell/(2D)$. Put
$d=\operatorname{ord}(\xi)$ and $u=d|t|$, so $0<u<\ell/2$.
If $t>0$, write $\Gamma=\{e^{is}:\alpha\le s\le\beta\}$ with
$0<\alpha<\beta<2\pi$ and $\beta-\alpha=\ell$. The integer
$k=\lceil\alpha/u\rceil$ satisfies
\[
   \alpha\le ku<\alpha+u<\beta,
   \qquad ku<2\pi.
\]
If $t<0$, use the reflected arc $\overline\Gamma$ in the same construction.
In both cases, with $n=dk$ we obtain
\[
   \eta^n=e^{int}\in\Gamma,
   \qquad n\operatorname{dist}(\eta,E)\le n|\eta-\xi|
      \le n|t|=ku<2\pi.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:symbol-direct-divdiff} yields
\[
   \operatorname{dist}(\eta,E)\|R(\eta,T)\|
      \le\frac{2\pi ML_w}{a-q}.
\]
Thus the supremum of the boundary resolvent expression on
$\mathbb T\setminus E$ is at most
\[
   B:=ML_w\max\left\{\frac{2\pi}{a-q},\frac{2N}{g}\right\},
\]
with the stated convention when $F_0=\emptyset$.

To pass to the exterior, let $\lambda=r\eta$, where $r>1$ and
$\eta\in\mathbb T$. If $\eta\notin E$, the resolvent identity and
$\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le M/(r-1)$ give
\[
   \|R(\lambda,T)\|
      \le\bigl(1+(r-1)\|R(\lambda,T)\|\bigr)
             \|R(\eta,T)\|
      \le(1+M)\|R(\eta,T)\|.
\]
Since $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\le(r-1)+\operatorname{dist}(\eta,E)$, it follows that
\[
   \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le M+(1+M)B.
\]
If $\eta\in E$, then $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E)=r-1$ and the Neumann estimate
gives the smaller bound $M$. This proves \eqref{eq:symbol-constructive}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:symbol-certificate}
The scalar data in Theorem~\ref{thm:symbol-constructive} involve only
finitely many root orders and powers. Indeed, any root of order
$m>2\pi/\ell$ has a power in $\Gamma$, and hence cannot belong to
$E(w,q)$. Thus $E(w,q)$ can be determined by testing the finitely many
orders $m\le\lfloor2\pi/\ell\rfloor$. Having determined $E$, the
search over $N$ in the theorem terminates. For a polynomial symbol,
the remaining minima are minima of explicitly given continuous
functions of one angular variable.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:symbol-threshold}
Let $w\in A^{1,1}(\mathbb D)$, let $Q\in(0,\|w\|_\infty)$ be a peripheral
threshold, and fix $M_0\ge1$. Set
\[
   E_+=E(w,Q),\qquad
   E_-:=\{\xi\in E_+:b_w(\xi)<Q\},\qquad
                                                     
   A=M_0 L_w \max_{\xi\in E_+}\operatorname{ord}(\xi).
\]
Let $C_+=C(w,Q,M_0)$ be the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:symbol-constructive} obtained at level $Q$, with $M$ replaced
by $M_0$ and any admissible scalar data. There exists $q_0<Q$ such that
$E(w,q)=E_-$ for $q_0\le q<Q$. For every power bounded $T$ satisfying
\[
   M(T)\le M_0,
   \qquad \sup_{n\ge1}\|w(T^n)\|\le q,
   \qquad q_0\le q<Q,
\]
the following estimates hold, after increasing $q_0$ if necessary:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $E_-\ne\emptyset$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symbol-threshold-bound}
   K_{E_-}(T)\le\frac{6AC_+}{Q-q}.
\end{equation}
\item If $E_-=\emptyset$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symbol-empty-threshold}
   \sup_{|\lambda|\ge1}\|R(\lambda,T)\|
       \le\frac{2AC_+}{Q-q},
   \qquad r(T)\le1-\frac{Q-q}{2AC_+}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The finiteness of $E_+$ implies that the numbers $b_w(\xi)<Q$ for
$\xi\in E_+$ have a common upper bound strictly below $Q$. Choosing
$q_0\in[0,Q)$ above that bound gives $E(w,q)=E_-$ for
$q_0\le q<Q$; when $E_-$ is empty there is no lower bound to impose.
Since $Q$ is a threshold strictly below $\|w\|_\infty$, the symbol
$w$ is nonconstant, so $L_w>0$ and $A>0$. Increase $q_0$ so that
$Q-q_0\le2A$.

Put $\varepsilon=Q-q$ and $\delta=\varepsilon/(2A)\le1$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:symbol-constructive}, applied at level $Q$, gives
$K_{E_+}(T)\le C_+$; the displayed formula for $C_+$ also shows
$C_+\ge M_0\ge1$. For every $\xi\in E_+\setminus E_-$, some
$n\le\operatorname{ord}(\xi)$ satisfies $|w(\xi^n)|=Q$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:symbol-direct-divdiff} gives
\[
   \|R(\xi,T)\|\le\frac{M(T)L_wn}{\varepsilon}
      \le\frac A\varepsilon.
\]
The resolvent Neumann series therefore implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symbol-root-removal}
   \|R(\lambda,T)\|\le\frac{2A}{\varepsilon}
   \quad\text{if}\quad
   |\lambda-\xi|\le\delta,
   \quad \xi\in E_+\setminus E_-.
\end{equation}

Suppose first that $E_-\ne\emptyset$. Inside any of these discs,
$|\lambda|\le2$ and hence $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_-)\le3$, so
\eqref{eq:symbol-root-removal} gives
\[
   \operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_-)\|R(\lambda,T)\|
      \le\frac{6A}{\varepsilon}.
\]
Outside all the discs, let $|\lambda|>1$ and choose a nearest point
of $E_+$ to $\lambda$. If this point belongs to $E_-$, the required
resolvent expression is at most $C_+$. Otherwise
$d:=\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_+)\ge\delta$ and
$\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_-)\le d+2$, so the expression is at most
\[
   C_+\left(1+\frac2d\right)
      \le C_+\left(1+\frac{4A}{\varepsilon}\right)
      \le\frac{6AC_+}{\varepsilon}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:symbol-threshold-bound}.

If $E_-=\emptyset$, every point of $E_+$ has been removed. Outside
the discs we have $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,E_+)\ge\delta$, giving
$\|R(\lambda,T)\|\le2AC_+/\varepsilon$ for $|\lambda|>1$.
Inside the discs use \eqref{eq:symbol-root-removal}. The structure
theorem gives $r(T)<1$, so continuity extends the bound to $|\lambda|=1$.
For each $\eta\in\mathbb T$, the disc centred at $\eta$ of radius
$1/\|R(\eta,T)\|$ is contained in the resolvent set. Consequently
every spectral point $z$ satisfies
$1-|z|\ge\varepsilon/(2AC_+)$, by choosing $\eta=z/|z|$ when $z\ne0$.
The same inequality for $z=0$ follows from
$\varepsilon/(2AC_+)\le1$. This proves
\eqref{eq:symbol-empty-threshold}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:generalsymbolnecessity}
Let $V\ne0$ satisfy $V^2=0$, put $T=I+V$, and take
$w(z)=(1-z)^2$. Then $T^n=I+nV$ and $w(T^n)=0$ for every $n\ge1$,
so the norm-gap condition holds with $q=0<\|w\|_\infty=4$ and
$E(w,0)=\{1\}$. Nevertheless $T$ is not power bounded, and therefore
is not Ritt. Thus the power-boundedness hypothesis in
Theorem~\ref{thm:generalsymbolstructure} cannot be omitted.

The peripheral set for a general symbol may contain roots of even
order. For instance, $T=-I$ and $w(z)=1-z^2$ satisfy $w(T^n)=0$
for every $n$; here $E(w,0)=\{1,-1\}$ and $T^2=I$ is Ritt.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:jamison}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $c(\mathbf n)\le c<\infty$, then $J(\mathbf n)\ge2\sin\frac{\pi}{c+1}$.
\item For $n_k=b^k$ with an integer $b\ge2$, $J(\mathbf n)=2\sin\frac{\pi}{b+1}$; for $\mathbf n=\mathbb N$, $J(\mathbf n)=\sqrt3$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
See Proposition~1.4 in \cite{BDG}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:arcsampling}
Let $c_\infty(\mathbf n)<\infty$, let $c'\ge c_\infty(\mathbf n)$, and let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ be power bounded with $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$. Suppose that one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\displaystyle\sup_{k\ge0}\ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma_{c'}}\|(\eta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|<\infty$;
\item $\displaystyle\sup_{k\ge0}\|w(T^{n_k})\|<m_{\Gamma_{c'}}(w)$ for some $w\in A^{1,1}(\mathbb D)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $T$ is a Ritt operator. Here $\Gamma_1=\{-1\}$. The arc $\Gamma_{c'}$ may be replaced by any closed arc $\{e^{it}:\alpha\le t\le\gamma\}\subset\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ satisfying \eqref{eq:arccond} with $c'$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
In case (ii), Lemma~\ref{lem:divdiff} applied to $S=T^{n_k}$ gives (i). Let $K$ be the uniform bound in (i). For $\eta'\in\mathbb T$ with $\operatorname{dist}(\eta',\Gamma_{c'})\le\frac1{2K}$, the Neumann series gives $\eta'\in\rho(T^{n_k})$ and $\|(\eta'-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|\le2K$ for all $k$. Choose $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac1{2K}]$ so small that the closed $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood $\Gamma'$ of $\Gamma_{c'}$ in $\mathbb T$ does not contain $1$; then $\Gamma'$ is a closed arc $\{e^{it}:\alpha'\le t\le\gamma'\}$ with $\alpha'<\frac{2\pi}{c'+1}$ and $\gamma'>\frac{2\pi c'}{c'+1}$, so both ratios in \eqref{eq:arccond} computed for $\Gamma'$ are strictly larger than $c'$. Choose $c''$ with
\[
   c'<c''\le\min\Big\{\frac{\gamma'}{\alpha'},\ \frac{2\pi-\alpha'}{2\pi-\gamma'}\Big\};
\]
then $\Gamma'$ satisfies \eqref{eq:arccond} with $c''$, and $c''>c'\ge c_\infty(\mathbf n)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:subseq} shows that $(\{n_k\},\Gamma')$ has the sampling property, and Proposition~\ref{thm:general} applies. The same enlargement increases both ratios of a general arc, and the argument includes $c'=1$, where $\Gamma_1=\{-1\}$ and $\Gamma'$ is a small arc around $-1$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:sparse}
Let $T\in\mathcal B(X)$ be power bounded.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item If $n_{k+1}/n_k\to1$, $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$, and $\sup_k\|(\zeta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|<\infty$ for one point $\zeta\in\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$, then $T$ is a Ritt operator.
\item Suppose $n_0=1$. If $c(\mathbf n)\le c<\infty$ and $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|<2\sin\frac{\pi}{c+1}$, then $T$ is a Ritt operator.
\item If $c_\infty(\mathbf n)<\infty$, $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$ and $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|<2\sin\frac{\pi}{c_\infty(\mathbf n)+1}$, then $T$ is a Ritt operator.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
(a) Let $K=\sup_k\|(\zeta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|$, $\varepsilon=\frac12\min\{1/(2K),|\zeta-1|\}$, and let $\Gamma=\{e^{it}:\alpha\le t\le\gamma\}$ be the arc $\{\eta:|\eta-\zeta|\le\varepsilon\}$; by the Neumann series $\|(\eta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|\le2K$ for $\eta\in\Gamma$. Both ratios in \eqref{eq:arccond} are $>1$, so \eqref{eq:arccond} holds with $c'=1=c_\infty(\mathbf n)$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:arcsampling}(i) applies.

(b) Let $q=\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|<2\sin\frac{\pi}{c+1}\le J(\mathbf n)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:jamison}). If $\lambda\in\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T$, then $|\lambda^{n_k}-1|\le\|I-T^{n_k}\|\le q$ for all $k$, so $\lambda=1$ by the definition of $J(\mathbf n)$. Since $c_\infty(\mathbf n)\le c$, we have $q<2\sin\frac{\pi}{c+1}\le2\sin\frac{\pi}{c_\infty(\mathbf n)+1}=m_{\Gamma_{c_\infty(\mathbf n)}}(1-z)$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:arcsampling}(ii) applies with $w(z)=1-z$ and $c'=c_\infty(\mathbf n)$. (c) is proved in a similar way.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:n0}
(a) The normalisation $n_0=1$ is essential in (b), through the Jamison constant: for $n_k=2\cdot3^k$ one has $c(\mathbf n)=3$, but $T=-I$ satisfies $T^{n_k}=I$ for all $k$, so that $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|=0$ while $T$ is not Ritt; here $J(\mathbf n)=0$. Theorem~\ref{thm:arcsampling} and parts (a), (c), which carry the spectral hypothesis, do not use $n_0=1$.

(b) In (b) the power-boundedness assumption is superfluous when the gaps of $\mathbf n$ are bounded: if $G:=\sup_k(n_{k+1}-n_k)<\infty$ and $A:=\sup_k\|T^{n_k}\|<\infty$, then $M(T)\le\max\{1,A\max_{0\le r<G}\|T^r\|\}$, since every $n\ge1$ can be written as $n=n_k+r$ with $0\le r<G$; and a sampled displacement bound $q$ gives $A\le1+q$.

(c) A one-point resolvent bound along $(T^{n_k})$ detects the Ritt property whenever $n_{k+1}/n_k\to1$ (for instance for $n_k=(k+1)^2$, or along the primes after adjoining $1$), while for geometric sequences an arc of prescribed logarithmic length is needed. The next result shows that for $n_k=b^k$ the arc $\Gamma_b$ is optimal among arcs symmetric about $-1$, even under the spectral hypothesis $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$, and determines the sharp norm thresholds.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:sharp}
Let $b\ge2$ be an integer and $n_k=b^k$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Let $\Gamma$ be a closed arc contained in the interior of $\Gamma_b$, i.e.\ $\Gamma\subset\{e^{it}:\frac{2\pi}{b+1}<t<\frac{2\pi b}{b+1}\}$. There is a normal contraction $T$ on $\ell^2$ with $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$, which is not a Ritt operator, such that
\[
   \sup_{k\ge0}\ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}\|(\eta-T^{b^k})^{-1}\|<\infty
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   \sup_{k\ge0}\|I-T^{b^k}\|\le Q_b .
\]
\item Among power bounded operators with $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$, the implication
$\sup_k\|I-T^{b^k}\|<Q\ \Rightarrow\ T$ Ritt holds for $Q=Q_b$, and it fails for every $Q>Q_b$; it also fails if $<Q_b$ is replaced by $\le Q_b$, even for normal contractions on $\ell^2$.
\item Without the spectral assumption the sharp threshold is $2\sin\frac{\pi}{b+1}$: the implication $\sup_k\|I-T^{b^k}\|<2\sin\frac\pi{b+1}\Rightarrow T$ Ritt holds for every power bounded $T$, and the scalar operator $T=e^{2\pi i/(b+1)}$ has $\sup_k|1-T^{b^k}|=2\sin\frac{\pi}{b+1}$ and is not Ritt.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
(i) Put $\alpha=2\pi/(b+1)$, choose $c_m\in(0,1]$ with $c_m\to0$, and let
\[
   \theta_m=\alpha b^{-m},\qquad \rho_m=e^{-c_m\theta_m},\qquad \mu_m=\rho_me^{i\theta_m}\qquad(m\ge1).
\]
Let $T$ be the diagonal operator on $\ell^2$ with eigenvalues $\mu_m$. Then $T$ is a normal contraction, $\mu_m\to1$, and $\sigma(T)=\{\mu_m:m\ge1\}\cup\{1\}\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$. Since $1-|\mu_m|\le c_m\theta_m$ while $|1-\mu_m|\ge\rho_m\sin\theta_m\ge\theta_m/\pi$ for large $m$, we have $|1-\mu_m|/(1-|\mu_m|)\to\infty$, so $\sigma(T)$ is contained in no Stolz domain $\{|1-\lambda|\le C(1-|\lambda|)\}\cup\{1\}$, and $T$ is not Ritt \cite{LeMerdy}.

Fix $k\ge0$. If $k\ge m$, then $b^k\theta_m=\alpha b^{k-m}$ and $b^{k-m}\equiv(-1)^{k-m}\pmod{b+1}$, so $\mu_m^{b^k}=\rho_m^{b^k}e^{\pm i\alpha}$ lies on one of the radii $R_\pm=\{\rho e^{\pm i\alpha}:0\le\rho\le1\}$. If $k<m$, then $b^k\theta_m=\alpha b^{-(m-k)}\in(0,\alpha/b]$, so $\mu_m^{b^k}$ lies in the closed sector $S=\{\rho e^{is}:0\le\rho\le1,\ 0\le s\le\alpha/b\}$. Hence $\sigma(T^{b^k})\subset R_+\cup R_-\cup S\cup\{1\}=:F$ for every $k$. The compact set $F$ meets $\mathbb T$ exactly in $\{e^{\pm i\alpha}\}\cup\{e^{is}:0\le s\le\alpha/b\}$, which is disjoint from $\Gamma$; since $\Gamma\subset\mathbb T$, the compact sets $\Gamma$ and $F$ are disjoint and $d:=\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,F)>0$. As $T^{b^k}$ is normal, $\|(\eta-T^{b^k})^{-1}\|=1/\operatorname{dist}(\eta,\sigma(T^{b^k}))\le1/d$ for all $\eta\in\Gamma$ and all $k$.

For $0\le\rho\le1$ and $z\in\mathbb T$, writing $1-\rho z=(1-\rho)\cdot1+\rho(1-z)$ gives
$|1-\rho z|\le(1-\rho)+\rho|1-z|\le\max\{1,|1-z|\}$.
All the unimodular directions just encountered satisfy $|1-z|\le2\sin(\alpha/2)=2\sin\frac\pi{b+1}$. Therefore every sampled eigenvalue satisfies $|1-\mu_m^{b^k}|\le Q_b$, and $\|I-T^{b^k}\|=\sup_m|1-\mu_m^{b^k}|\le Q_b$ by normality. In fact the supremum over $k$ equals $Q_b$: taking $k=m$ gives $\mu_m^{b^m}=e^{-\alpha c_m}e^{i\alpha}\to e^{i\alpha}$, while fixing $m$ and letting $k\to\infty$ gives $\mu_m^{b^k}\to0$. These yield the lower bounds $2\sin(\alpha/2)$ and $1$, respectively.

(ii) When $Q_b>1$, i.e.\ $b\le4$, sufficiency for $Q=Q_b$ is Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse}(c) with $c_\infty(\mathbf n)=b$; when $Q_b=1$ it is Lemma~\ref{lem:subone} below. The operator of (i) has $\sup_k\|I-T^{b^k}\|\le Q_b<Q$ for every $Q>Q_b$ and is not Ritt, which proves both failure assertions.

(iii) Sufficiency is Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse}(b) with $c=b$; the scalar example follows from $b^k\equiv(-1)^k\pmod{b+1}$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:offcentre}
The position of the arc matters in the optimality statement for $\Gamma_2$.
The shorter arc
\[
 A=\{e^{it}:\pi/2\le t\le\pi\}
\]
also gives a dyadic resolvent criterion: if $T$ is power bounded,
$\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$ and
\[
 \sup_k\sup_{\eta\in A}\|R(\eta,T^{2^k})\|<\infty,
\]
then $T$ is Ritt.
Indeed, a Neumann series argument extends this uniform bound to
\[
 A_\delta=\{e^{2\pi it}:1/4-\delta\le t\le1/2+\delta\}
\]
for some $0<\delta<1/8$. We verify the sampling property for this enlarged arc.
Given $0<|\theta|<\pi/2$, put $u=|\theta|/(2\pi)$ and choose $m\ge0$
with $x=2^m u\in[1/4,1/2)$. For $\theta>0$ the time $2^m$ hits $A$.
For $\theta<0$, if $x\ge1/2-\delta$, then the phase $1-x$ belongs to
$[1/2,1/2+\delta]$. Otherwise the next phase is
$y=1-2x\in(2\delta,1/2]$. If $y\ge1/4$ it already belongs to the arc;
if $y<1/4$, choose the least $l\ge1$ with $2^ly\ge1/4$. Then
$2^ly<1/2$ and $2^l<1/(2y)<1/(4\delta)$.
Thus a chosen dyadic time $n$ always satisfies
\[
 e^{in\theta}\in A_\delta,\qquad n|\theta|\le\frac\pi{2\delta}.
\]
For the last case use $n|\theta|=4\pi 2^l x$; the earlier cases have
$n|\theta|<2\pi$. Proposition~\ref{thm:general} now applies.
Since the lengths of $A$ and $\Gamma_2$ are $\pi/2$ and $2\pi/3$,
respectively, Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}(i) cannot be interpreted as
minimality among all arcs of arbitrary position.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:subone}
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex Banach space, let
$n_k\to\infty$, and suppose that $\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}$.
If $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|<1$, then $T=I$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Put $q=\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|<1$.
For every $\lambda\in\sigma(T)$, spectral mapping gives
$|1-\lambda^{n_k}|\le q$ for all $k$.
If $|\lambda|<1$, the left-hand side tends to $1$; if
$|\lambda|>1$, it tends to infinity. Thus $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb T$,
and the peripheral spectral assumption gives $\sigma(T)=\{1\}$.

The principal logarithm $L=\log T$ is therefore defined by the
holomorphic functional calculus. For each positive integer $n$, the
identity $\log(z^n)=n\log z$ holds on a sufficiently small
neighbourhood of $1$. Since $\sigma(T)=\sigma(T^n)=\{1\}$, the
composition rule for this calculus consequently gives
$\log(T^n)=nL$. In particular,
\[
 n_k L=\log(T^{n_k})
 =-\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{(I-T^{n_k})^j}{j},
\]
where the series converges in norm and represents the principal
logarithm because $\|I-T^{n_k}\|\le q<1$. Hence
\[
 n_k\|L\|\le\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{q^j}{j}
 =-\log(1-q).
\]
Letting $k\to\infty$ yields $L=0$, and the functional calculus
identity $T=e^L$ gives $T=I$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:unbounded}
Let $c(\mathbf n)=\infty$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every closed arc $\Gamma\subset\mathbb T\setminus\{1\}$ there is a normal contraction $T$ on $\ell^2$ with $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$ and $\sup_k\sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}\|(\eta-T^{n_k})^{-1}\|<\infty$ which is not Ritt.
\item For every $q>1$ there is a normal contraction $T$ on $\ell^2$ with $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$ and $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|\le q$ which is not Ritt.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
(i) Let $d=\operatorname{dist}(1,\Gamma)>0$. Since the quotients are unbounded, we may choose indices $K(1)<K(2)<\cdots$ with $K(j)\ge1$ and $n_{K(j)}/n_{K(j)-1}\ge16j\log2/d$; then $K(j)\ge j$ and $n_{K(j)-1}\ge n_{j-1}\ge j$. Put $\varepsilon_j=\log2/n_{K(j)}$, $\theta_j=j\varepsilon_j$, $\mu_j=(1-\varepsilon_j)e^{i\theta_j}$, and let $T$ be diagonal with eigenvalues $\mu_j$. We have
\[
   \theta_j=\frac{j\log2}{n_{K(j)}}\le\frac{j\log2\,d}{16j\log2\,n_{K(j)-1}}=\frac{d}{16n_{K(j)-1}}\le\frac d{16j}\to0
\]
and $\varepsilon_j\to0$, so $\mu_j\to1$ and $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$; moreover $|1-\mu_j|/(1-|\mu_j|)\ge(1-\varepsilon_j)\sin(\theta_j)/\varepsilon_j\gtrsim j\to\infty$, so $T$ is not Ritt. Fix $j$ and $k$. If $k\ge K(j)$, then $|\mu_j^{n_k}|\le(1-\varepsilon_j)^{n_{K(j)}}\le e^{-\log2}=\frac12$, so $|\eta-\mu_j^{n_k}|\ge\frac12$ for $\eta\in\mathbb T$. If $k<K(j)$, then $n_k\varepsilon_j\le n_{K(j)-1}\varepsilon_j\le d/(16j)$ and $n_k\theta_j\le d/16$, so $|\mu_j^{n_k}-1|\le|(1-\varepsilon_j)^{n_k}-1|+|e^{in_k\theta_j}-1|\le n_k\varepsilon_j+n_k\theta_j\le d/8$ and $|\eta-\mu_j^{n_k}|\ge d-d/8$ for $\eta\in\Gamma$. Together with $\operatorname{dist}(\eta,1)\ge d$, this gives $\operatorname{dist}(\eta,\sigma(T^{n_k}))\ge\min\{\frac12,\frac{7d}8\}$ for all $\eta\in\Gamma$ and $k$, and normality gives the uniform resolvent bound.

(ii) We may assume $1<q<2$. Put $\tau=(q-1)/2\in(0,\frac12)$, $L=\log(1/\tau)$, $\rho_m=e^{-L/n_{m+1}}$, $\theta_m=\tau/n_m$ and $\lambda_m=\rho_me^{i\theta_m}$, $m\ge0$, and let $T$ be diagonal with eigenvalues $\lambda_m$; then $T$ is a normal contraction with $\lambda_m\to1$, so $\sigma(T)\subset\mathbb D\cup\{1\}$. Fix $k$ and $m$. If $k\le m$, then $n_k\le n_m$, $\rho_m^{n_k}\ge\rho_m^{n_m}=e^{-Ln_m/n_{m+1}}\ge e^{-L}=\tau$, and
\[
   |1-\lambda_m^{n_k}|\le(1-\rho_m^{n_k})+|1-e^{in_k\theta_m}|\le(1-\tau)+n_m\theta_m=(1-\tau)+\tau=1 .
\]
If $k\ge m+1$, then $|\lambda_m|^{n_k}\le\rho_m^{n_{m+1}}=\tau$ and $|1-\lambda_m^{n_k}|\le1+\tau<q$. Hence $\sup_k\|I-T^{n_k}\|\le q$ by normality. Finally, using $1-e^{-x}\le x$, $|1-\lambda_m|/(1-|\lambda_m|)\ge\rho_m\sin(\theta_m)\,n_{m+1}/L\ge(\tau/(\pi L))\,n_{m+1}/n_m$ for large $m$, which is unbounded since $c(\mathbf n)=\infty$; so $T$ is not Ritt.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:rittsampling}
$\mathbf n$ is a Ritt sampling sequence if and only if $c(\mathbf n)<\infty$. If $c(\mathbf n)<\infty$, then for every power bounded $T$,
\[
   \sup_{n\ge1}n\|T^n-T^{n-1}\|\le M(T)\,c(\mathbf n)\,\sup_{k\ge0}n_k\|T^{n_k}-T^{n_k-1}\| .
\]
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Suppose $c(\mathbf n)<\infty$ and let $A=\sup_kn_k\|T^{n_k-1}(I-T)\|$. For $n\ge1$ choose $k$ with $n_k\le n<n_{k+1}$; then $T^{n-1}(I-T)=T^{n-n_k}T^{n_k-1}(I-T)$ and $n\|T^{n-1}(I-T)\|\le M(T)\frac{n}{n_k}\,n_k\|T^{n_k-1}(I-T)\|\le M(T)c(\mathbf n)A$.

Conversely, suppose $c(\mathbf n)=\infty$ and choose indices $k_m$ with $R_m:=n_{k_m+1}/n_{k_m}\to\infty$; put $p_m=n_{k_m}$, $q_m=n_{k_m+1}$, $N_m=\sqrt{p_mq_m}=p_m\sqrt{R_m}$, $L_m=R_m^{1/4}$ and $\lambda_m=\exp(-1/N_m+iL_m/N_m)$. Since $L_m/N_m=R_m^{-1/4}/p_m\to0$, $\lambda_m\to1$, and $|\lambda_m|<1$. Let $T$ be the diagonal contraction on $\ell^2$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_m$. For $n\ge1$ and $x=n/N_m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diagbound}
   n|\lambda_m|^{n-1}|1-\lambda_m|\le n\,e^{-(n-1)/N_m}\Big(\frac1{N_m}+\frac{L_m}{N_m}\Big)\le2e\,L_m\,xe^{-x},
\end{equation}
using $|1-\lambda_m|\le|1-e^{-1/N_m}|+|1-e^{iL_m/N_m}|$, $L_m\ge1$ and $e^{1/N_m}\le e$. If $n=n_k\le p_m$, then $x\le p_m/N_m=R_m^{-1/2}$ and $n|\lambda_m|^{n-1}|1-\lambda_m|\le2eL_mR_m^{-1/2}=2eR_m^{-1/4}\le2e$. If $n=n_k\ge q_m$, then $x\ge R_m^{1/2}\ge1$, $xe^{-x}$ is decreasing on $[1,\infty)$, and $n|\lambda_m|^{n-1}|1-\lambda_m|\le2eR_m^{3/4}e^{-R_m^{1/2}}$, which is bounded. As no $n_k$ lies strictly between $p_m$ and $q_m$, we get $\sup_k\sup_mn_k|\lambda_m|^{n_k-1}|1-\lambda_m|<\infty$, i.e.\ $\sup_kn_k\|T^{n_k}-T^{n_k-1}\|<\infty$. On the other hand, for $n=\lfloor N_m\rfloor$ we have $x\in(1/2,1]$ for large $m$, $|1-\lambda_m|\ge|\operatorname{Im}\lambda_m|\ge e^{-1/N_m}\frac2\pi\frac{L_m}{N_m}$, and $n|\lambda_m|^{n-1}|1-\lambda_m|\ge\frac{N_m}{2}e^{-1}\cdot\frac{2L_m}{e\pi N_m}=\frac{L_m}{e^2\pi}\to\infty$. Hence $\sup_nn\|T^n-T^{n-1}\|=\infty$ and $T$ is not Ritt.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:fractional}
Let $s>0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $c(\mathbf n)<\infty$, then every power bounded $T$ satisfies
\[
 \sup_{n\ge1}n^s\|T^{n-1}B^s\|\le M(T)c(\mathbf n)^s\sup_kn_k^s\|T^{n_k-1}B^s\|,
\]
and if the right-hand side is finite, then $T$ is a Ritt operator.
\item If $c(\mathbf n)=\infty$, the diagonal contraction $T$ constructed in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:rittsampling} satisfies $\sup_kn_k^s\|T^{n_k-1}B^s\|<\infty$, and it is
not a Ritt operator.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
(i) The interpolation inequality is proved exactly as in Theorem~\ref{thm:rittsampling}, writing $T^{n-1}B^s=T^{n-n_k}T^{n_k-1}B^s$ for $n_k\le n<n_{k+1}$. Suppose now that $A:=\sup_nn^s\|T^{n-1}B^s\|<\infty$ and choose an integer $l$ with $ls>1$. For $n\ge2$ write $n-1=l(k-1)+r$ with $0\le r<l$, so that $k\ge1$ and $k\ge(n-1)/l\ge n/(2l)$. Commutativity gives
\[
 T^{n-1}B^{ls}=T^r\big(T^{k-1}B^s\big)^l,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 \|T^{n-1}B^{ls}\|\le M(T)\Big(\frac{A}{k^s}\Big)^l\le M(T)A^l(2l)^{ls}n^{-ls}.
\]
The moment inequality \eqref{eq:moment} with $s_1=1$, $s_2=ls$, applied to $y=T^{n-1}x$, yields
\[
 \|T^{n-1}Bx\|\le C_{1,ls}\,(M(T)\|x\|)^{1-1/(ls)}\big(M(T)A^l(2l)^{ls}n^{-ls}\|x\|\big)^{1/(ls)}\lesssim n^{-1}\|x\|,
\]
so $\sup_nn\|T^{n-1}(I-T)\|<\infty$ and $T$ is Ritt.

(ii) For the diagonal operator $T$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_m$, the operator $B^s$ is diagonal with eigenvalues $(1-\lambda_m)^s$ (principal branch, $\operatorname{Re}(1-\lambda_m)>0$), so $\|T^{n-1}B^s\|=\sup_m|\lambda_m|^{n-1}|1-\lambda_m|^s$. As in \eqref{eq:diagbound}, with $x=n/N_m$,
\[
 n^s|\lambda_m|^{n-1}|1-\lambda_m|^s\le n^se^{-(n-1)/N_m}\Big(\frac{2L_m}{N_m}\Big)^s\le2^se\,L_m^s\,x^se^{-x}.
\]
For $n=n_k\le p_m$ this is at most $2^seR_m^{s/4}R_m^{-s/2}\le2^se$; for $n=n_k\ge q_m$ we have $x\ge R_m^{1/2}$, and once $R_m^{1/2}\ge s$ the function $x^se^{-x}$ is decreasing on $[R_m^{1/2},\infty)$, so the bound is at most $2^seR_m^{3s/4}e^{-R_m^{1/2}}$, which is bounded in $m$. For each of the finitely many remaining coordinates, the supremum over all $n\ge1$ of $n^s|\lambda_m|^{n-1}|1-\lambda_m|^s$ is finite because $|\lambda_m|<1$. Since $T$ is not Ritt (Theorem~\ref{thm:rittsampling}), the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{samp:exact}
Fix $1<q<2$. The following assertions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every complex Banach space $X$ and every power bounded
operator $T\in\mathcal B(X)$,
\begin{equation}\label{samp:hypotheses}
 \sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\|I-T^n\|\le q,
 \qquad \sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\}
\end{equation}
imply that $T$ is a Ritt operator.
\item The same implication holds for every normal contraction on $\ell^2$.
\item $q<\alpha(\mathcal N)$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, when $1<\alpha(\mathcal N)<2$, the implication fails
at $q=\alpha(\mathcal N)$, already for a diagonal contraction on $\ell^2$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Assume (iii), and choose $q_1$ with
$q<q_1<\alpha(\mathcal N)$. By \eqref{samp:escape}, there are
$B>0$ and $\delta\in(0,\pi)$ such that for each $0<t<\delta$ one can
choose $n\in\mathcal N$ satisfying
$nt\le B$ and $|1-e^{int}|>q_1$.
Let $T$ satisfy \eqref{samp:hypotheses}, and set $M=M(T)$.
For $\xi=e^{it}$ or $e^{-it}$, the decomposition
\[
 \xi^n-T^n=(\xi^n-1)I+(I-T^n)
\]
and the Neumann series give
\[
 \|R(\xi^n,T^n)\|\le\frac1{q_1-q}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} consequently yields
\begin{equation}\label{samp:local-resolvent}
 |\xi-1|\,\|R(\xi,T)\|
 \le\frac{Mn|\xi-1|}{q_1-q}
 \le\frac{MB}{q_1-q}
 \qquad(0<|\arg\xi|<\delta).
\end{equation}
The peripheral spectral assumption ensures that the resolvent is bounded
on the remaining compact arc
$\{\xi\in\mathbb T:|\arg\xi|\ge\delta\}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary}
now shows that $T$ is Ritt. This proves (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i), and
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is immediate.

To prove (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii), suppose that
$\alpha(\mathcal N)\le q$. Choose an increasing sequence $B_j\to\infty$
so large that, with $\varepsilon_j=B_j^{-1/2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{samp:damping-choice}
 \varepsilon_j\le\frac1{36},\qquad
 1+e^{-\sqrt{B_j}}\le q \qquad(j\ge1).
\end{equation}
For each $j$,
$\liminf_{t\downarrow0}h_{\mathcal N}(B_j,t)\le\alpha(\mathcal N)\le q$.
We may therefore choose $1>\theta_1>\theta_2>\cdots\downarrow0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{samp:bad-angles}
 h_{\mathcal N}(B_j,\theta_j)
 \le q+B_j^{-1}=q+\varepsilon_j^2.
\end{equation}
Define a diagonal contraction on $\ell^2$ by
\begin{equation}\label{samp:diagonal}
 T e_j=z_j e_j,\qquad
 z_j=\exp(-\varepsilon_j\theta_j+i\theta_j).
\end{equation}

We first verify the displacement bound for every coordinate and every
sampling time. Fix $j$ and $n\in\mathcal N$, and abbreviate
\[
 B=B_j,\quad \varepsilon=\varepsilon_j,\quad
 t=n\theta_j,\quad r=e^{-\varepsilon t}.
                     
\]
If $t>B$, then
\[
 |1-z_j^n|\le1+r\le1+e^{-\varepsilon B}
 =1+e^{-\sqrt B}\le q.
\]
Suppose next that $t\le B$, so that $|1-e^{it}|\le q+\varepsilon^2$ by
\eqref{samp:bad-angles}. If $|1-e^{it}|\le q$, radial convexity gives
\[
 |1-re^{it}|\le(1-r)+r|1-e^{it}|\le q,
\]
since $q>1$. It remains to consider $|1-e^{it}|>q$. Since $|1-e^{it}|\le t$, we have
$t>q$ and hence $0\le r\le r_*:=e^{-q\varepsilon}$.
The identity
\[
 |1-re^{it}|^2=r|1-e^{it}|^2+(1-r)^2
\]
and convexity of the right-hand side as a function of $r$ show that
\begin{equation}\label{samp:convex-bound}
 |1-re^{it}|^2
 \le\max\bigl\{1,\ r_*(q+\varepsilon^2)^2+(1-r_*)^2\bigr\}.
\end{equation}
Put $a=1-r_*$. Since $q\varepsilon\le1$, the elementary inequalities
$x/2\le1-e^{-x}\le x$ for $0\le x\le1$ give
$q\varepsilon/2\le a\le q\varepsilon$. Therefore
\begin{align*}
 r_*(q+\varepsilon^2)^2+(1-r_*)^2-q^2
 &=-aq^2+r_*(2q\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^4)+a^2\\
 &\le-\frac{q^3\varepsilon}{2}
       +(q^2+2q)\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^4\\
 &\le-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+9\varepsilon^2
 \le-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}<0.
\end{align*}
Here we used $1<q<2$ and $\varepsilon\le1/36$.
Together with \eqref{samp:convex-bound}, this proves
$|1-z_j^n|\le q$ in the remaining case. Taking suprema over $j$ and $n$
gives $\sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\|I-T^n\|\le q$.

Finally, $|z_j|<1$ and $z_j\to1$, so
$\sigma(T)=\{z_j:j\ge1\}\cup\{1\}$ and
$\sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T=\{1\}$. Nevertheless,
\begin{align*}
 |e^{i\theta_j}-1|\,\|R(e^{i\theta_j},T)\|
 &\ge\frac{|e^{i\theta_j}-1|}{|e^{i\theta_j}-z_j|}
 =\frac{|e^{i\theta_j}-1|}{1-e^{-\varepsilon_j\theta_j}}\\
 &\ge\frac{2\theta_j/\pi}{\varepsilon_j\theta_j}
 =\frac{2}{\pi\varepsilon_j}\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{align*}
Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary} shows that $T$ is not Ritt, contradicting
(ii). This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{samp:full-threshold}
The following assertions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Every power bounded operator $T$ on every complex Banach space
satisfying
\[
 \sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\|I-T^n\|<2,
 \qquad \sigma(T)\cap\mathbb T\subset\{1\},
\]
is a Ritt operator.
\item $\alpha(\mathcal N)=2$.
\item For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $L\in\mathbb N$ and $x_0>0$ such
that for every real $x\ge x_0$ there exist $n\in\mathcal N$ and a
positive odd integer $m\le L$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{samp:odd-approximation}
 |n-mx|<\varepsilon x.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Assertion \textup{(i)} is unchanged if it is restricted to normal
contractions on $\ell^2$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
If (ii) holds and $Q:=\sup_{n\in\mathcal N}\|I-T^n\|<2$, choose
